_comment: Backfill for r20261107-1504 (bench 5: the telcoin-network main branch at 4bf4604d2 with the nine instrumentation commits of r20261105-0803 and 29 topic commits, branch bench/main-fixes-2026-11 at 067639def; same fleet, operator scripts, parameters and chaos plan as r20261105-0803; a light-load arm of three blasts, indices 0-2, before the headline blast, which is index 4 because index 3 aborted; metrics from the run's own bench-obs Prometheus), published with: make_bundle.py --run r20261107-1504 --compare r20261105-0803 --floor-blast-dir blast-0-20261107T163112Z --backfill benchmark/report/backfill/2026-11-07-main-fixes.json. Sources (field by field in benchmark/private/bench5-r20261107-1504/P/backfill-notes.md): the run manifest (harness, node_probe, node_startup incl. db_sync_mode and fsync_probe, consensus_parameters, admission, coordinated_start, chaos, chaos_schedule, chaos_schedule_refresh, blast, blasts, blasters, obs, prom_window, fleet_ready, log_rate, cert_failures, timestamps, commit_stalls_sampled), metrics.json (Prometheus 15 s from bench-obs, 15:40:20Z to 18:39:18Z, plus Cloud Monitoring 60 s), the Prometheus snapshot taken at teardown, the generators' results and sampled landings of indices 0, 1, 2 and 4, the eleven nodes' unit logs, the analysis units A1 (KPIs, windows, light arm), A2 (certification and vote path), A3 (F1 and F3 verdicts, recovery, boundaries), A4n (census and the execution split), A4o (timeline, faults, defects) and A6 (land-path stages and levers), the run's analysis brief and the cherry-pick ledger. recovery: node, killed_utc, restarted_utc, rejoined_utc and catch_up_secs equal what make_bundle computes from the node-mode metric (rejoined 18:23:05Z, 1,365 s), so merge_recovery keeps them silently; failed_reports (0) comes from validator-05's own log and fills the computed null (no seal-failure series for that node). The log's own times (promotion 18:22:49.980, restart to active 1,385.8 s, kill to active 28 min 05.8 s) are in the caveats. harness is not set: harness_block uses the manifest's record (538af51, dirty) and ignores the backfill. generator.analysis_sha is left to make_bundle.
title: The main branch with the commit-lag, rejoin and execution fixes
summary: We repeated the chaos run of 5 November (r20261105-0803) on the same fleet: ten c3-highcpu-8 validators with Hyperdisk Balanced disks, one in each of ten regions, and an observer. The node was built from the main branch plus 29 commits written after that run. With them, consensus commits no longer wait for the validator's own execution, a restarted validator rejoins once at the network head, the execution engine logs less and recovers signers off its main thread, and new log lines time every stage of a transaction's path. Before the usual 40-minute load, three short light blasts measured the floor. With 8 senders per generator, the median transaction reached a block timestamp 0.25 s after it was sent, and its generator saw the receipt after 1.63 s. Under full load, with all ten generators running, average chain throughput was 3,449 tx/s, 24.7 % below the 4,578 tx/s of r20261105-0803. The median time to land was 2.81 s (3.3 s there) and the 95th percentile 14.40 s (12.84 s). The median time until a generator saw its receipt was 14.18 s (12.92 s). Executing a transaction got 47 % cheaper, but the database commit after each consensus output took about 1.05 s instead of 0.3 s, with the same logical writes and about four times the bytes on disk, so throughput was bound by persisting. The cause lies below the execution engine and is not yet known. No healthy validator left the committee (two did on r20261105-0803). The killed validator rejoined once, 28 minutes after the kill and a minute or two after the load ended; on r20261105-0803 it went through 13 promotions. One of the new commits backfired. A validator now refuses to vote for a header that names a block it has not executed yet, so the three fastest executors, Tokyo, Hong Kong and Mumbai, had almost none of their headers certified, and their generators landed nothing for 8 to 14 minutes before the kill. At light load, London's and the Netherlands' transactions landed in bursts about 20 s apart.

evidence_detail: Commit 067639def is the head of the branch bench/main-fixes-2026-11, built for this benchmark from the telcoin-network main branch at 4bf4604d2 (6 November), which already contains the lazy protocol negotiation of PR 1783. On top of main it carries the nine instrumentation commits of r20261105-0803, cherry-picked unchanged, and then 29 topic commits. Commit lag: consensus no longer waits for the validator's own execution before it commits, the fork check moves to the subscriber, and new gauges report the commit and execution lag. Rejoin: a validator that has fallen out rejoins only at the network head, after a grace period and at most twice an epoch; it refuses votes while it is inactive or while its own execution is behind the block a header names; it can rejoin from a stalled head, goes inactive when its restored DAG has a gap, and re-requests a stuck replay. Engine: the per-block and per-output debug dumps move to trace level, execution is timed in parts, signers are recovered off the execution thread, and reads are cached per consensus output. Land path: timing lines per batch, header, certificate and output; a batch builder that wakes when a transaction arrives; and the digests of a cancelled header are queued again for the next one. The run named the image by registry digest (adiri@sha256:a1a82341…, pushed as adiri:bench-main-fixes-20261107).

fleet.label: c3-highcpu-8 + Hyperdisk Balanced (c3-hdb), ten regions, validator-05 in Ashburn

load.placement: one blaster per validator, in that validator's zone, sending only to it

methodology: The node image was built for this benchmark from the branch bench/main-fixes-2026-11 (telcoin-network main plus the nine instrumentation commits of r20261105-0803 and 29 topic commits) and named by registry digest (sha256:a1a82341…). Before creating anything the harness ran that image to confirm that it reports telcoin-network 0.1.0 built from commit 067639def, has the sub-second timestamp fork active from genesis and contains the log messages later checks rely on. The committed consensus parameters were unchanged from r20261105-0803: maximum header delay 1,000 ms, minimum header delay 350 ms, maximum batch delay 250 ms and a header batch threshold of 5.

The analysis reads fixed-shape log lines and Prometheus series, not free text. The instrumentation of r20261105-0803 is unchanged: the voter's vote path by stage, the proposer's vote round trips, the engine's execute, persist and commit timings, rejoin blockers and node-mode transitions with their reasons, the scheduled leader of every round, batch-serve denials, epoch-record signers and request durations by service class. This build adds one line per batch (why it was built, how long its oldest transaction waited, its quorum and report times), per header (digests, the wait of its oldest digest, why it was proposed, and why a header was never certified), per committed certificate and sub-DAG (with the leader's creation time and the commit timestamp), and per consensus output (fetch, persist, the engine queue, and execution split into signer recovery, EVM, state root and finish). It also adds the commit-lag and execution-lag gauges, rejoin attempts and holds, vote refusals and their reasons.

Preflight checked access, tools, quotas and a clean genesis directory, and confirmed the load-generator image built from tn-transaction-generator commit 6dad96f (sha256:5766094d…). This build records, per landed transaction, both the block timestamp (whole seconds, the basis of time to land) and the moment the generator's own block scanner saw the receipt (time to seen, what a user waits for), by submission phase. It also exports a 1-in-100 sample of landings with each block's batch and consensus position. The KPI driver used for this page reproduces every published KPI of r20261105-0803, r20261103-1922, r20261007-0316 and r20261006-0458 exactly.

The harness created ten validators and one observer on c3-highcpu-8 (8 vCPU, 16 GB), each with a 100 GB Hyperdisk Balanced boot disk provisioned at 20,000 IOPS and 800 MiB/s, one validator in each of ten regions (Los Angeles, London, Sydney, Tokyo, Ashburn, the Netherlands, Singapore, Hong Kong, Seoul and Mumbai) with the observer in Los Angeles, the zones of r20261105-0803; every node was created on the first attempt. It also created the run's own metrics VM (bench-obs, e2-standard-4, 50 GB, in Los Angeles) running Prometheus and Grafana; it collects metrics only, no logs.

As on r20261105-0803, each node's keys were generated on the node by the operator scripts of the v0.2.0-devnet release (the v2 scripts), four nodes at a time, with each node advertising its RPC endpoint on its internal address. The harness built genesis for a separate benchmark chain (chain id 32286, 20-minute epochs) and, before any node started, installed on every node a network configuration in Closed admission mode that names every validator and lists the observer as trusted by every validator.

Each node was finalized by the release's scripts, four at a time, and stopped again. While every node was stopped, the harness wrote the benchmark settings into each start script, with the log filter of r20261105-0803 (info, with debug for the primary, the engine, the subscriber, worker networking and request-response), and ran a short fsync probe on each node's disk (fleet median 986 µs; slowest validator-06, 1,253 µs). The harness now records each node's database sync mode: every node ran the default durable mode, which syncs the database on every commit. Because this build logs the engine's dumps at trace, the same filter wrote 8 to 11 MB a minute on validator-01 during the light blasts and about 5 MB a minute under load, against 1.16 GB a minute on r20261105-0803.

All eleven nodes were started at one due time, 15:23:30 UTC, in the same second, on the first attempt. Each node's metrics agent was then pointed at bench-obs; no node was restarted for it. The devnet's shared observability VM received none of this run's samples or logs.

A verify-only pass read back from each running node its commit (067639def), fork schedule, start-script settings and parameters, and all eleven passed by 15:37:37 UTC. The health and admission gate, which finished at 15:40:20, found all eleven nodes reporting to bench-obs with no devnet series, all ten validators active, and on every node Closed admission on the primary and worker networks with no fallback and no denied connection.
The harness deployed the devnet contract set that the mixed workload calls from 15:40:20 to 15:50:47 UTC. The chain was then idle until 16:01:58.

The light-load arm came first, with chaos off. One-off funder VMs, one per planned blast, funded the senders of all four (16:03 to 16:10:48 UTC). Ten generators, one per validator in that validator's zone and sending only to it, then ran three blasts in turn, each with 60 s of warm-up, 360 s of mixed load and 60 s of cool-down: index 0 with 8 senders per generator and up to 16 transactions in flight per sender (mixed load 16:16:56 to 16:22:56), index 1 with 16 senders and the same window (16:36:54 to 16:42:54), and index 2 with 600 senders and a window of 4 (16:56:55 to 17:02:55). Each blast's results were archived in a directory of their own.

The fourth blast, index 3, was the full load profile. Creating one of its ten generator VMs failed at about 17:18 UTC when the gcloud client timed out after 300 s, and the harness stopped the blast at 17:20:07. The nine generators already created had sent for at most about 90 s, all inside their warm-up, and the chaos had not fired. Their partial results are kept but used nowhere on this page. Following the harness's printed resume instruction, the operator funded a fresh set of senders (17:30:25 to 17:32:50) and ran the same profile again as index 4, which is the headline blast.

In index 4 ten generators on e2-standard-2, each with 600 senders and a window of 16 (at most 96,000 transactions in flight), started together at 17:38:02 UTC: a preamble of setup transactions, 120 s of warm-up, 2,400 s of the mixed load of r20261105-0803 and up to 180 s of cool-down. Measured from the generators' own phase records, the merged mixed window ran from 17:40:15 to 18:21:01 and the window with all ten generators running from 17:41:01 to 18:20:15. No network delay was injected.

The chaos schedule was timed to the chain's epochs. The harness read the ConsensusRegistry at a pinned block (block 15,099, epoch 6), chose the close of epoch 7, and re-read the schedule at 17:39:03 UTC (drift 0 s). bench-validator-05's container was killed with SIGKILL at 17:54:44, 59 s before that close, and held down; the node was restarted at 17:59:44 and the observer at 18:04:44. Before the kill and the observer restart each node saved its own container log.

The harness sampled the fleet's highest block during the run. The only period it recorded without a new block, 18:21:00 to 18:22:30 UTC, is the end of the load, not a stall. Afterwards it collected each generator's results and the on-node sampler files and waited for every validator to read active (validator-05 already did at the first poll). It pulled 60-second machine metrics from Cloud Monitoring and 15-second node metrics from bench-obs's Prometheus (15:40:20 to 18:39:18 UTC), with no series missing; collection finished at 18:41:19.

The KPIs and windows on this page come from the publishing pipeline's own window and KPI steps, run through the driver that reproduced the comparison runs. Windows are cut from the generators' own phase records, not the planned phase times. The floor KPIs read index 0. The bias-free time to commit joins the landing sample to each block's millisecond commit timestamp from validator-01's log. The stage breakdown of a transaction's path, certification, the vote path, the F1 and F3 checks, the execution split and the log census come from the log lines above, read from every node's complete unit log in one streaming pass each, and from a local replay of the Prometheus snapshot taken at teardown.

Teardown pulled every node's logs before deleting anything. With the engine dumps at trace, the unit logs of all eleven nodes came to about 1.87 GB together (about 49 GB each on r20261105-0803), and the pulls took five minutes (18:43:54 to 18:48:54 UTC). The teardown then ran the certification check, took a 20 MB snapshot of the bench-obs Prometheus, checked provenance (commit 067639def and the sub-second fork on every node) and deleted all 12 instances at 19:17:24, in one attempt (TEARDOWN_DONE deleted=12 left=0). The results directory was re-indexed: 804 files, 2.64 GB. The whole run took 4 h 12 min, against 9 h 16 min for r20261105-0803.
caveats: The comparison run, r20261105-0803, had the same fleet in the same zones, the same load shape and chaos plan, the same consensus timing (1,000/350/250 ms) and the same operator scripts. The node build differs by the 29 topic commits and a newer main underneath. The generator build differs (6dad96f against 3911723; it adds records). The log volume differs about 200-fold, and here the load followed an hour of light blasts. Against r20261105-0803, average chain throughput with all generators running fell from 4,578 to 3,449 tx/s (-24.7 %), blocks a second from 15.84 to 12.96, while primary rounds a second rose from 0.84-0.91 to 0.97-1.00, so each round carried fewer blocks. The median time to land fell from 3.3 to 2.81 s, the 95th percentile rose from 12.84 to 14.40 s, and the median time to seen rose from 12.92 to 14.18 s (95th percentile 29.78 to 53.39 s). No difference can be assigned to any one change.

The headline blast is index 4, not index 3. Index 3 aborted when one gcloud call to create a generator VM timed out on the client, before the chaos fired and with every generator still in its warm-up. Its partial results are excluded from every figure. The re-run started 20 minutes later than planned (17:38:02 instead of 17:17:36 UTC), with the same profile and a freshly funded set of senders. A single transient client timeout aborting a blast is a harness defect, the third run in a row with this class of fault.

Throughput fell because persisting got slower, not executing. Per transaction the engine spent 288.6 µs (215 µs on r20261105-0803): 87.4 µs executing and 199.2 µs persisting, about four times the persist cost there. The inverse, about 3,465 tx/s, matches the chain's rate. Most of the persist time (178 of 199 µs) is the database commit and its sync, 1.03 to 1.06 s per consensus output on every node against 0.30 to 0.34 s there. The logical writes per transaction were the same in both runs (table growth 73, 33 and 47 bytes per transaction; 0.44 accounts and 0.62 storage slots touched), but each transaction cost about 4.3 times the device bytes (155 KB against 36 KB). The disks wrote 470 to 530 MB/s sustained, with one-minute peaks at the 800 MiB/s provisioned limit, while CPU stayed at 17 to 19 %. The disk type, provisioning, OS image family and operator scripts were the same. r20261103-1922 showed the same write pattern, so r20261105-0803 looks like the outlier. The cause lies below the execution engine and has not been found. One untested difference: r20261105-0803 also wrote a 1.16 GB-a-minute debug log to the same volume.

Executing got 47 % cheaper per transaction (87.4 against about 165 µs). The engine dumps are gone from the hot path (0.2 to 0.3 µs per transaction now). Waiting for signer recovery fell to almost nothing, because recovery runs off the execution thread. Of the rest, the EVM took 26.5 µs, the state root 49.2 µs (56 % of execution, so a parallel state root is the next execution step) and finishing a block 11.4 µs. The queue of consensus outputs in front of the engine never held more than two: consensus committed at the rate execution finished (on validator-01 before the kill, 0.573 sub-DAGs committed against 0.559 outputs executed a second).

One of this build's commits starved three validators' users under load. Before voting, a validator now waits up to 1 s for its own execution to reach the block a header names, and then refuses. Tokyo, Hong Kong and Mumbai executed fastest (6.4 to 9.1 rounds of execution lag, against 12.6 to 13.5 for the middle of the fleet and 22 to 31 for Los Angeles, Sydney and Ashburn), so their headers named blocks the others had not executed yet. Seven voters refused each of their headers 537 to 683 times. The other seven validators' certificates were exactly a quorum, so every round moved on and the three headers were cancelled (Tokyo's in 916 of 918 rounds). Under load they had 0.2 %, 0.0 % and 16.3 % of their own headers certified, against 99.7 to 100 % for the other seven and about 100 % for all ten at idle and light load. Their generators got no RPC error, but landed nothing for 802, 853 and 491 s before the kill. They started landing again 7 to 13 s after it, when, with nine voters left, rounds had to wait for a fast node's certificate; Hong Kong stalled again for 227 s from 18:05:43 UTC. The refusal is a regression of this build, to be dropped or revised before it reaches main.

Not every generator landed transactions all the time. No generator got the 'validator is inactive' error before the kill (two did on r20261105-0803, after their validators were demoted). But besides the three starved generators of the last caveat, generator 05 landed nothing for the first 193 s of its mixed phase, and its warm-up transactions were seen after 318 s at the median. After the kill it stayed pinned to its down and then inactive validator and landed nothing more. These stalls make the 99th-percentile time to land 402.56 s; that figure measures the stalls, not ordinary latency.

The floor KPIs come from the light blasts, not the load: index 0 (8 senders per generator) is the published floor, passed to the pipeline with --floor-blast-dir. Index 1 (16 senders) gives nearly the same: land 0.31 s, seen 1.73 s. The light windows are short (358 s of all ten generators each), came before the load and include no epoch boundary and no chaos. At that load every sender's window is full, so throughput there (694 and 1,291 tx/s) is set by the window and the latency, not by the chain. The block timestamp is whole seconds and rounds down: on the landing sample a transaction reached its leader's commit timestamp after 0.64 s at the median and was seen after 1.50 s; the mean rounding bias there was 440 ms.

The 600 x 4 point comes from index 2: 600 senders per generator with a window of 4, at most 24,000 in flight, with no chaos and a 324-s window. It carried 3,868.5 tx/s, 12 % more than the load blast, with a median time to land of 0.88 s and to seen of 3.22 s. By Little's law its mean time to seen (4.79 s) implies 18,544 transactions in flight, 77 % of the cap. The load blast, with four times the window, held about 82,000 in flight for less throughput. Past about 24,000 in flight, a larger window adds queueing, not throughput, but the comparison is not clean: the load blast includes the chaos, two epoch boundaries and the starved generators.

At light load London's and the Netherlands' generators landed at a median of 12.8 and 13.6 s (index 0) and 11.3 and 17.0 s (index 1), while the other eight landed in 0.12 to 0.84 s. Their headers were certified (99.5 %), but only 13 to 18 % of their certificates were committed. The rest waited for the periodic re-send of undelivered headers, about every 20 s and within 10 ms of each other on the two nodes, so their transactions landed in bursts; in index 0 both generators landed nothing for the same 41 s. The pooled floor median is not affected, but the floor's 95th and 99th percentiles are theirs. At 600 x 4 they landed in 1.39 and 1.51 s. This is the far-validator certificate inclusion seen on earlier runs, not a change of this build.

Because the block timestamp rounds down to the second, the page also gives a time to land with 0.5 s added (3.31 s at the median under load). The landing sample, 1 in 100 joined on validator-01's log, gives a bias-free median time to commit of 3.07 s and a 95th percentile of 13.42 s, with a mean rounding bias of exactly 500 ms. The commit timestamp is the leader header's creation time, so it reads earlier than the commit itself; validator-01 logged the commit itself 4.70 s after submission at the median.

Under load the time to seen sits about ten seconds above the commit. Before the kill a consensus output waited 9.6 s at the median in the engine's queue, 64 % of the time to seen, because executing and persisting one output took 1.66 s, of which the database commit took 1.04 s. Persisting is off the visibility path (blocks reach RPC once executed) and reaches the user only through that queue. Los Angeles, Sydney and Ashburn executed 2 to 3 % slower than the chain committed (94 to 97 µs per transaction against 84 to 88, all in finishing blocks and signer recovery), so their backlog grew. That accounts for 9 to 13 s of the 21 to 35 s by which their generators' receipts trailed the landing. Why finishing is slower there is not known. At light load consensus took 82 % of the time to seen; its largest stage, from the leader's header to the commit, took 0.61 s at the median (40 %).

No healthy validator left the committee. On r20261105-0803 two did, when their own commit fell 41 rounds behind; here commit no longer waits for execution. Execution fell up to 62 rounds behind on Los Angeles, 54 on Sydney and 58 on Seoul (during index 2), and every one of them stayed active. Before the kill the commit lag stayed at or below 5 rounds at the 99th percentile (6.12 at most during the chaos window), and all ten validators were active until the kill. The wait moved to the subscriber: on Los Angeles a consensus output waited 14 s at the median for its execution before it was assembled.

Validator-05 restarted at 17:59:44 UTC with 212 certificates restored and no gap in its stored DAG. Because it was killed 59 s before an epoch close, it found itself an epoch behind 19 s later and followed the chain as an inactive member. Under load it barely gained: 165 outputs behind at 18:00:37, it replayed about 30.5 outputs a minute while the chain made 23.3. It made one rejoin attempt, at a gap of 20 rounds, at 18:22:49.65, was active 0.3 s later and had its first own certificate committed 1.85 s after that: 28 min 05.8 s after the kill, a minute or two after the mixed load ended, in the middle of epoch 9. r20261105-0803's validator-05 needed 13 promotions and the next epoch boundary. The check 'active within 2 minutes of the kill' is not met, but inconclusive: catch-up was bound by execution under saturation. While inactive, the node re-requested a stuck replay 8 times, and its replay never froze.

The recovery record on this page takes its rejoin time (18:23:05 UTC) and catch-up duration (1,365 s, from the first inactive sample) from the 15-second node-mode samples. Validator-05's own log puts the demotion at 18:00:03.5, the promotion at 18:22:49.98 and restart to active at 1,385.8 s. The failed-report count (0) is from the log; the node has no seal-failure series in the metrics.

With validator-05 down, nine validators voted. The kill paused commits for about 13 s, and the epoch-7 close 59 s later left the chain 24 s without a block with transactions (13 s on r20261105-0803); the epoch-8 close left 14 s. Los Angeles and Sydney reached each loaded close 11 to 27 s late and never signed the epoch-7 and epoch-8 records, so both were signed by exactly seven validators, the quorum with no margin. After the kill those two refused 14,785 and 11,953 votes as execution-behind, so every remaining voter was on the critical path and commits paused 4 to 15 s at a time from 18:16 to 18:21. No runbook restart was needed.

The nodes logged 77,168 warnings and errors (266,118 on r20261105-0803), with no panic and no database error, and the storm of 'too new' vote refusals is gone (12 against 100,852). Two new messages appeared at the loaded epoch-8 boundary and are open questions: about 1,400 'failed to track spawned task' messages (1,248 inside the chaos window) and 414,513 transactions skipped as 'nonce too low' (about 37,700 per node). The batch-serve pool never filled; 6,675 batch-sync streams were refused at open, all after the epoch-8 boundary.

The validators did less CPU work than on r20261105-0803 (busiest p95 22.2 % against 36.7 %) and wrote more: the telcoin process wrote 498.7 MiB/s at the median (131.6 MiB/s there) and I/O pressure peaked at 30.7 to 34.2 % (10.2 to 17.4 %). These figures include almost no logging, where r20261105-0803's included 25 to 45 MB/s of debug log. The pre-start fsync probe does not predict persist time: validator-06, the slowest probe, committed in 1,079 ms at the median against 1,069 to 1,081 ms for the fleet.

The node metrics on this page come from the run's own Prometheus on bench-obs, scraped every 15 s. The analysis behind the caveats also replays the snapshot of that Prometheus taken at teardown. No sample or log line of this run went to the devnet's shared observability VM.

The harness is recorded at commit 538af51, marked dirty; the dirty flag is a known false positive of the harness's record and was not re-checked for this run. The run's planned phase times differ from the generators' real ones by up to 77 s, so the analysis cuts every window from the generators' own records. No node was restarted outside the chaos plan.
This configuration has been run once, so run-to-run variation is not measured.
